en.title: async/await Internals: State Machine, Task vs ValueTask, Continuations, ConfigureAwait

options.text: Line A throws `ArgumentNullException` synchronously, because the throw happens before the first `await` and therefore runs on the caller's thread.
Line A returns a faulted task; line B throws an `AggregateException` whose `InnerException` is the `ArgumentNullException`.
Line A completes normally and returns a task whose `Status` is `Faulted`; the `ArgumentNullException` is thrown at line B, unwrapped.
Line A returns a task whose `Status` is `Canceled`, because the state machine aborts before reaching its first `await`.

en.explanation: The body of an `async` method runs inside the generated `MoveNext`, whose `try/catch` catches every exception and forwards it to `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder.SetException`, so the caller always gets a task back and the exception surfaces only when that task is awaited; `TaskAwaiter.GetResult` rethrows the original exception, not a wrapper. The 'throws synchronously' option is half right (the code does run on the caller's thread before the first `await`) but draws the wrong conclusion: the exception is caught by the state machine, not propagated to the call site; you only get eager throwing by validating in a non-`async` wrapper method. The `AggregateException` option confuses `await` with `.Wait()`/`.Result`, which are the APIs that wrap in `AggregateException`. The `Canceled` option is wrong because only an `OperationCanceledException` produces a `Canceled` task; any other exception produces `Faulted`.

options.text: It is fine: like `Task<int>`, a completed `ValueTask<int>` caches its result, because the struct stores the value in its own result field once `GetResult` has run, so `second` equals `first` without re-running the read.
Undefined behaviour: the pooled source may already have been reset or reused after the first `GetResult`, so the second `await` can throw or observe another operation's result.
The second `await` transparently restarts the read: a `ValueTask<int>` is a deferred operation like `Func<Task<int>>`, so `second` receives the next chunk of data from the reader.
It does not compile: since C# 11 the compiler tracks single-consumption awaitables and reports an error when a `ValueTask<T>` local is awaited a second time.

en.explanation: `ValueTask<T>` is a single-consumption handle: when it wraps an `IValueTaskSource<T>`, the first `GetResult` call is the signal for the source to recycle itself, so any further `await`, `.Result` access, or concurrent await is outside the contract and may observe another operation's state. The fix is to call `AsTask()` (or `Preserve()`, .NET 5+) *instead of* the first `await` when multiple consumers are needed; calling it after `vt` has already been consumed is just as invalid on a pooled source. The 'caches its result' option is the misconception that `ValueTask` is a cheaper `Task`: the struct does hold an inline result field, but only when it was created from a plain value or wraps a real `Task<T>`; when it wraps an `IValueTaskSource<T>` the result lives in the (recyclable) source, and callers cannot know which backing they got. The 'restarts the read' option treats `ValueTask` like a lazy `Func<Task<T>>`; the operation started when `ReadAsync` was called and the struct only represents that one operation. The 'does not compile' option is wrong because no C# version tracks how many times an awaitable is awaited; the rule is enforced by documentation and analyzers (CA2012), not by the language.

en.prompt: Which statement about `await task.ConfigureAwait(false)` is true on .NET 10?

options.text: It guarantees the continuation runs on a thread-pool thread, because the awaiter queues `MoveNext` through `ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem` instead of running it inline, even when `task` is already completed.
It stops both the `SynchronizationContext` and the `ExecutionContext` from flowing, which is why `AsyncLocal<T>` values set before the `await` are no longer visible after it in ASP.NET Core.

It is required in ASP.NET Core request handlers: the `AspNetCoreSynchronizationContext` admits one thread per request, so a caller blocking with `.Result` deadlocks unless the continuation is released from that context.
It only controls whether the awaiter captures `SynchronizationContext.Current`/`TaskScheduler.Current`; `ExecutionContext` still flows and an already-completed `task` never yields.

en.explanation: `ConfigureAwait(false)` changes one bit passed to the awaiter: whether to capture the current `SynchronizationContext` (or non-default `TaskScheduler`) when registering the continuation. Everything else stays: `ExecutionContext` is captured by the method builder independently, so `AsyncLocal<T>` flows; and when the awaited task is already complete, `IsCompleted` returns `true` and the state machine keeps running inline without any scheduling, on the current thread. The `UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem` option is the 'moves to the thread pool' misconception with an invented mechanism: nothing is queued by the awaiter, the continuation runs on whichever thread completes the task (inline, unless that thread has a non-default context or the task was created with `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`), and a completed task never yields; `ConfigureAwaitOptions.ForceYielding` (.NET 8) is the API for forcing a yield. The 'stops both contexts' option is wrong because `ExecutionContext` flow is not affected by `ConfigureAwait`; suppressing it needs `ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow`. The deadlock option is wrong because ASP.NET Core has no `SynchronizationContext` at all (there is no `AspNetCoreSynchronizationContext` type), so `ConfigureAwait(false)` cannot prevent a deadlock there; the classic deadlock belonged to `AspNetSynchronizationContext` in ASP.NET on .NET Framework, which Core removed.

en.prompt: An `async Task<int> CountAsync()` method (Release build, .NET 10) is called and every awaited operation happens to be already completed by the time it is awaited, so the method never suspends. Which statement about allocations is true?

options.text: The state machine struct is never boxed; the only possible heap allocation is the returned `Task<int>`, and even that is skipped for cached results such as `-1..8`, `true`/`false` or `null`.
The state machine is boxed on the heap as soon as the method is invoked, because `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder.Start` needs a reference-type instance to hold hoisted locals.
Nothing is allocated at all, because `Task<int>` is a struct that carries the result inline when the method completes synchronously.
Two allocations always occur, the boxed state machine and the `Task<int>`; since .NET Core 2.1 they are merged into one object, so the synchronous path costs a single allocation.

en.explanation: In Release builds the compiler emits the state machine as a struct, `Start` runs `MoveNext` on the caller's stack, and boxing happens only inside `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted`, i.e. on the first awaiter whose `IsCompleted` is `false`. A method that never suspends therefore allocates at most the `Task<int>` result object, which `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>` serves from a static cache for `bool`, small `int` values (-1 to 8) and `null` reference results. The 'boxed as soon as invoked' option describes Debug builds (where the state machine is a class) and generalises it to Release, which is wrong. The 'nothing is allocated' option confuses `Task<int>` with `ValueTask<int>`: `Task<T>` is a class, so a non-cached result always costs an object; `ValueTask<T>` is the type that carries a synchronous result inline. The 'two allocations merged into one' option correctly describes the .NET Core 2.1 `AsyncStateMachineBox` optimisation but applies it to the wrong path: the box-that-is-the-task exists only when the method actually suspends.

Model answer: the compiler turns `M` into an `IAsyncStateMachine` struct (state, `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<int>`, hoisted `a`, awaiter fields) and `Start` runs `MoveNext` synchronously on the calling thread-pool thread; `await A()` sees `awaiter.IsCompleted == true`, so no continuation is registered and the code continues inline with no allocation. At `await B()` the state is saved, the awaiter is stored in its field, `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted` boxes the machine once (the box is the returned `Task<int>` since .NET Core 2.1, so `M` allocates nothing before that point) and registers `MoveNext` as the continuation, capturing `ExecutionContext` always and `SynchronizationContext`/`TaskScheduler` only if present, which in ASP.NET Core they are not, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` changes nothing observable. When `B()` completes, its completing thread runs `MoveNext` inline (or posts it to the captured context, or queues it to the thread pool if the completing thread has a non-default context); `MoveNext` re-enters at the saved state, copies the awaiter out of its field, clears the field to `default`, resets the state to `-1`, and `GetResult` returns `b` or rethrows the original exception. `return a + b` becomes `SetResult`; any exception is caught in `MoveNext` and stored via `SetException`, reaching the caller unwrapped at its `await`.
rubric: Describes the compiler-generated `IAsyncStateMachine` (struct in Release) with a state field, an `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<int>`, hoisted locals (`a`) and awaiter fields, and that `MoveNext` runs synchronously on the calling thread-pool thread through `await A()` because the awaiter reports `IsCompleted == true`, so no continuation is registered for `A()`.

Explains that at `await B()` the state is saved and `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted` boxes the state machine exactly once (since .NET Core 2.1 the box is the `Task<int>` object itself) and registers `MoveNext` as the continuation via `UnsafeOnCompleted`; `M` itself allocates nothing before that point, and a separate `Task<int>` would only be allocated if the method completed without ever suspending (and even then cached results avoid it).

States that the continuation runs on the thread that completes `B()` (inline, or posted to a captured `SynchronizationContext`/`TaskScheduler`), that `ExecutionContext` always flows, and that in ASP.NET Core there is no `SynchronizationContext`, so `ConfigureAwait(false)` only skips the capture check and changes nothing observable here.

Explains completion: `return a + b` becomes `builder.SetResult`, an exception thrown anywhere in the body is caught in `MoveNext` and becomes `SetException` (faulted task, `OperationCanceledException` makes it canceled), and the caller's `await` rethrows the original exception via `GetResult` rather than an `AggregateException`.

Describes resumption mechanics: `MoveNext` re-enters at the saved state number, copies the awaiter out of its hoisted field, clears that field to `default` and resets the state to `-1` before calling `awaiter.GetResult()` to obtain `b`.

concepts.title: SynchronizationContext and the Classic ASP.NET Deadlock

en.title: SynchronizationContext and the Classic ASP.NET Deadlock

options.text: The request completes normally but slowly: `.Result` forces `LoadAsync` to execute synchronously on the request thread, so the awaited HTTP call degrades to ordinary blocking I/O and returns as soon as the response arrives.

`.Result` throws an `AggregateException` wrapping an `InvalidOperationException`, because the task-friendly `AspNetSynchronizationContext` detects a blocking wait on an incomplete task from a synchronous action and rejects it.

The request never completes on its own: the request thread blocks in `.Result` while owning the exclusive `AspNetSynchronizationContext`, and the posted continuation cannot acquire that context until the execution timeout aborts the thread.

The request stalls because the response is delivered on an I/O completion thread that cannot re-enter the controller instance, since `HttpClient` may only complete its task on the thread that started the call.

en.explanation: The request thread enters `Index` inside the per-request `AspNetSynchronizationContext`, which lets only one thread run in the request at a time. `LoadAsync` hits an incomplete task at `await`, captures that context (no `ConfigureAwait(false)`), and returns an incomplete `Task<string>`. `.Result` then blocks the request thread without releasing the context. When the HTTP response arrives, the continuation is `Post`ed to the context, which waits for the blocked thread: a two-party deadlock. It is not literally infinite in production: `Index` is a synchronous action, so `<httpRuntime executionTimeout>` (110 s by default when `debug="false"`) eventually aborts the thread with 'Request timed out'; with `debug="true"` the hang is unbounded. The 'slow but completes' option treats `await` as if it degraded to a synchronous call; the method really returns an incomplete task and the continuation really needs the context, so nothing makes progress. The `InvalidOperationException` option misplaces a real guard: `AspNetSynchronizationContext.OperationStarted` does throw 'An asynchronous operation cannot be started at this time' in synchronous stages, but it is called by `AsyncVoidMethodBuilder` (`async void`) and `RegisterAsyncTask`, never by a `Task`-returning async method, and blocking on a `Task` is never detected by the framework. The `HttpClient` option misattributes the cause: `HttpClient` is thread-safe and completes its task on whatever I/O thread it likes; that thread is free to run the continuation itself, but the awaiter routed the continuation to the request context, and that is the only reason it waits.

en.prompt: The same controller code (`LoadAsync().Result` with no `ConfigureAwait(false)` anywhere) is ported unchanged to an ASP.NET Core 10 MVC application on Kestrel. Why does the request return instead of hanging?

options.text: ASP.NET Core's request `SynchronizationContext` is multi-threaded: another pool thread is allowed to enter the request and run the continuation while the original thread is blocked in `.Result`, so the two never wait on each other.

ASP.NET Core installs no request `SynchronizationContext`: `SynchronizationContext.Current` is `null` on the request thread, so the awaiter captures nothing and the continuation runs on a free thread-pool thread while the request thread stays blocked.

Since .NET Core 3.0 the compiler emits `ConfigureAwait(false)` for every `await` in projects that reference the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` shared framework, so no context is captured anywhere in the call chain.

`HttpClient` on .NET Core completes its task on a dedicated I/O completion thread, and `TaskAwaiter` always runs the continuation inline on the completing thread regardless of any captured context, so the request thread is not needed.

en.explanation: ASP.NET Core removed the request context in 1.0. With `SynchronizationContext.Current == null` and the default `TaskScheduler`, the awaiter registers a plain continuation that runs on the thread pool (usually inline on the I/O thread that completed the task), so the task completes on another thread and unblocks `.Result`. The cost is a parked pool thread for the duration of the call: sync-over-async. The old hill-climbing injection adds threads slowly; since .NET 6 the portable thread pool notices `Task.Wait`/`.Result` on a worker (`NotifyThreadBlocked`) and injects compensating threads faster, but that is bounded by the max-thread count, each parked thread costs roughly 1 MB of stack, and throughput still degrades, so the correct fix remains async end to end. The 'multi-threaded context' option is a widespread misconception: there is no context at all, multi-threaded or otherwise. The 'compiler emits ConfigureAwait' option is wrong because `ConfigureAwait` is an ordinary method call the developer writes; neither Roslyn nor the SDK injects it (and in ASP.NET Core application code it would be a no-op anyway). The `HttpClient` option gets the mechanism backwards: the continuation runs inline on the completing thread *only because nothing was captured*; had a context been captured, `TaskAwaiter` would `Post` to it regardless of which thread completed the task, which is exactly what deadlocks classic ASP.NET.

options.text: No, it returns. `ConfigureAwait(false)` in `ReadJsonAsync` makes that method resume on a thread-pool thread, and `LoadAsync`'s continuation inherits the context of whichever thread completes `ReadJsonAsync`, which is the pool.
No, it returns. `ConfigureAwait(false)` applies to the whole call chain below the outermost `await` that uses it, so the inner setting propagates upward and `LoadAsync` resumes on the pool as well.
No, it returns. The WPF `Dispatcher` pumps queued continuations while a thread is blocked in `Task.Result`, so the posted continuation runs re-entrantly on the UI thread and the wait completes.

Yes, it hangs. `LoadAsync` awaits `ReadJsonAsync()` without `ConfigureAwait(false)`, so that `await` captures the `DispatcherSynchronizationContext`; the inner task completes on a pool thread, but `LoadAsync` resumes via the blocked UI thread.

en.explanation: The context is captured per `await`, on the thread that performs the `await`, at the moment it sees an incomplete task. `LoadAsync` runs on the UI thread, reaches `await ReadJsonAsync()` while the task is incomplete, and captures the `DispatcherSynchronizationContext`. Later `ReadJsonAsync` finishes on a pool thread (thanks to its `ConfigureAwait(false)`), which completes the inner task and triggers `LoadAsync`'s continuation, but that continuation was registered with the Dispatcher context, so it is posted to the UI thread, which is blocked in `.Result`. The 'inherits the completing thread's context' option reverses the mechanism: the completing thread's context is irrelevant; what matters is what was captured when the `await` was executed. The 'propagates upward' option is the 'ConfigureAwait is transitive' misconception; it configures exactly one awaiter and nothing else. The 'Dispatcher pumps' option is wrong because `Task.Result` blocks on a wait handle and does not run a Dispatcher frame; nothing is pumped, which is precisely why UI-thread blocking hangs.

en.prompt: On ASP.NET Core 10, in which of these hosting models does the framework still install a `SynchronizationContext` on the code path that runs your handler, so that a blocking `.Result` on an incomplete task inside that handler can hang exactly like classic ASP.NET did?

options.text: An MVC controller action: ASP.NET Core wraps each request in an `AspNetCoreSynchronizationContext` that serialises access to `HttpContext`, which is why `HttpContext` is documented as unsafe to touch from outside it.

A Minimal API endpoint delegate: because it runs as a lambda inside the routing middleware, the endpoint middleware installs a per-request context so that `HttpContext` and `IHttpContextAccessor` stay consistent across awaits.

A Blazor Server (interactive server) component: each circuit runs on a `RendererSynchronizationContext` that enforces a single logical thread, so blocking inside `OnInitializedAsync` or an event handler deadlocks the circuit.
A SignalR hub method: the hub dispatcher installs a per-connection `SynchronizationContext` so that invocations from one client are processed one at a time, in the order in which they were sent.

en.explanation: Blazor Server is the one place in ASP.NET Core that reintroduced a context: since ASP.NET Core 3.0 a circuit's rendering and event handling are serialised through a `RendererSynchronizationContext`, which is why the Blazor documentation forbids `.Result`, `.Wait()` and `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` in components. Blocking the logical thread while a captured continuation waits to be posted to it recreates the classic deadlock. The MVC and Minimal API options are wrong because controllers and endpoint delegates run with `SynchronizationContext.Current == null`; there is no `AspNetCoreSynchronizationContext` type, the middleware pipeline is a chain of plain async delegates on thread-pool threads, and `HttpContext` consistency across awaits comes from `AsyncLocal<T>`/`ExecutionContext`, not from a context (`HttpContext` is documented as not thread-safe precisely because nothing serialises access to it). The SignalR option is wrong because SignalR Core hubs do not install a context either; per-connection ordering comes from the connection's processing loop awaiting hub invocations sequentially (unless `MaximumParallelInvocationsPerClient` is raised), not from a `SynchronizationContext`.

en.prompt: A teammate is migrating an ASP.NET MVC 5 application that has several `.Result` and `.Wait()` calls to ASP.NET Core 10. They say: 'Those calls deadlocked on .NET Framework even after we sprinkled `ConfigureAwait(false)` in a few methods, but I tested on Core and they work, so we can leave them.' Explain, at the mechanism level, why the calls deadlocked in classic ASP.NET, why the partial `ConfigureAwait(false)` did not fix it there, why they no longer deadlock in ASP.NET Core, and what you would tell the teammate about leaving them in place. Mention any modern .NET hosting model where the original deadlock can still occur.
rubric: Explains the classic deadlock as a cycle: the request thread blocks in `.Result`/`.Wait()` while holding the exclusive `AspNetSynchronizationContext`, and the `await` continuation is posted to that same context, so neither side can proceed.

States that the context is captured at each `await` on the awaiting thread when the task is incomplete, and that `ConfigureAwait(false)` prevents the capture only for the specific `await` it is applied to, so one undecorated `await` in the chain is enough to keep the deadlock.

States that ASP.NET Core (since 1.0) installs no request `SynchronizationContext` (`SynchronizationContext.Current` is `null`), so continuations run on thread-pool threads and the blocked thread is eventually released.

Argues against leaving the calls: sync-over-async parks a thread-pool thread per call, degrades throughput and can starve the pool under load (compensating injection since .NET 6 is bounded), and the correct fix is to make the call chain `async` end to end, not `Task.Run(...).Result`.
Names at least one modern context where the deadlock still happens: Blazor Server's `RendererSynchronizationContext`, or a UI framework such as WPF/WinForms/MAUI with a single UI thread.
en.explanation: Model answer: in classic ASP.NET every request runs inside an exclusive `AspNetSynchronizationContext` (one thread at a time per request). An `await` on an incomplete task captures that context on the awaiting thread; `.Result` then blocks the request thread without releasing the context; when the I/O completes, the continuation is `Post`ed to the context and waits for the blocked thread, so both sides wait until `executionTimeout` aborts the thread. `ConfigureAwait(false)` avoids the capture only for the single `await` it decorates, so one undecorated `await` anywhere in the blocked chain reintroduces the hang; that is why sprinkling it in a few methods changed nothing. ASP.NET Core removed the request context in 1.0: `SynchronizationContext.Current` is `null`, continuations run on any free thread-pool thread (usually inline on the completing I/O thread), and the blocked thread is released. The calls should still be removed: each one parks a pool thread for the duration of the I/O (sync-over-async); the old hill-climbing injection is slow, and although the .NET 6+ thread pool compensates for `Task.Wait`-style blocking faster, that compensation is bounded, every parked thread costs roughly 1 MB of stack, and throughput drops under load. `Task.Run(...).Result` avoids the deadlock but still parks the request thread for the whole call and adds a pool hop. The deadlock is still reproducible today on any single-threaded context: WPF/WinForms/MAUI UI threads and Blazor Server circuits (`RendererSynchronizationContext`).

concepts.title: Task vs Thread and the Thread Pool

en.title: Task vs Thread and the Thread Pool

en.prompt: Which statement about `Task` and `Thread` in modern .NET (6 and later) is correct?

options.text: A `Task` may complete on any thread, but the pool reserves one worker per pending task so the continuation always has somewhere to run.
`Task.Run` usually creates a fresh OS thread; the pool mostly recycles stack memory and only reuses a thread when one happens to be idle.
A `Task` is a promise of a future result; it may be backed by a pool thread or by no thread at all while it is pending.
`await` on an incomplete task may yield to the caller, but it still parks the current thread at kernel level until the awaited work signals.

en.explanation: A `Task` is a handle to work that completes later; whether a thread is involved depends on what produced it. `Task.Run` queues a delegate to the pool, but an I/O task from `Stream.ReadAsync`, a timer task from `Task.Delay` or a `TaskCompletionSource` holds no thread while pending; the OS or a timer thread completes it and the continuation is queued as pool work. Option 1 is the classic conflation: nothing is reserved per pending task; awaiting 10,000 socket reads does not tie up 10,000 workers, and a continuation is queued only when the task actually completes. Option 2 is wrong because `Task.Run` enqueues a work item; the pool creates a thread only when it decides to grow (immediately below `ProcessorCount`, then slowly). Option 4 describes `.Wait()`/`.Result`, not `await`: `await` registers a continuation and returns control to the caller; the thread goes back to the pool and is not parked anywhere.

en.prompt: An ASP.NET Core endpoint calls a legacy SDK whose only API is synchronous and takes about 300 ms on a socket. A colleague changes the handler to `var r = await Task.Run(() => sdk.GetQuote(id));` and expects better throughput under load. What actually happens?

options.text: Throughput improves because the blocking call now runs on a background thread while the request thread returns to the pool and serves other requests.
Throughput improves because `Task.Run` uses the I/O completion thread pool, which is sized separately from the worker pool and grows faster under load.
The call becomes non-blocking: `Task.Run` converts synchronous work into an awaitable I/O operation, so no thread is held during the socket wait.
Throughput does not improve: the handler was already on a pool thread, so `Task.Run` blocks a different worker from the same pool for 300 ms and adds a hop.

en.explanation: Kestrel already dispatches each request onto a thread pool worker. `Task.Run` moves the synchronous call to another worker from the same pool, so the number of blocked pool threads under load is identical, plus an extra enqueue and context switch, and `HttpContext` is now reachable from a thread that may outlive the response. Option 1 is true only when the caller is a dedicated thread (a WPF/WinForms UI thread, a Blazor Hybrid render thread); on a server the 'request thread' returning to the pool gains nothing because the offloaded thread came from the same pool. Option 2 is wrong: `Task.Run` uses the worker threads; the I/O completion threads serve the OS completion path, and `Task.Run` never targets them. Option 3 is the core misconception: only a genuinely asynchronous API (one that hands the wait to the OS and completes via callback) frees a thread. Wrapping sync code in a task changes nothing about where the wait happens.

en.prompt: A .NET 8 API runs on an 8-core container. A burst of 2,000 concurrent requests arrives; each one calls a legacy SDK that performs a synchronous socket call taking about 500 ms (no shared lock, the calls are independent). The default `ThreadPool.MinThreads` is unchanged. What does the thread pool do during the burst?

options.text: It creates 8 workers immediately and then stops growing: the pool never exceeds `ProcessorCount` unless `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads` is called, so the remaining requests wait for a free worker.
It creates workers up to `ProcessorCount` at once, then injects about one thread per 500 ms while the queue stays non-empty and throughput does not improve; p99 latency spikes for tens of seconds.

It creates one thread per queued request up to the default maximum (32,767) within a few milliseconds, because the maximum is the target the pool grows toward, so latency is only briefly affected while the threads start.

Hill climbing detects the drop in throughput and immediately doubles the worker count; the .NET 6+ blocking-aware injection then sees the blocked socket calls and covers the rest of the burst almost instantly.

en.explanation: Below `ProcessorCount` (8 here) the pool creates a worker as soon as work arrives and nobody is idle. Above that, growth is slow: the starvation heuristic adds a thread at most about once per 500 ms, and when items are still trickling through, hill climbing takes over and is no faster. With 8 threads the pool drains about 16 requests per second, and each injected thread adds only two more per second, so a queue of 2,000 blocking calls takes tens of seconds to clear and p99 latency balloons; this is the textbook thread pool starvation signature in `dotnet-counters` (`threadpool-queue-length` climbing, `threadpool-thread-count` creeping up). Option 1 confuses the minimum with a maximum: `MinThreads` is the count the pool creates without hesitation, not a cap; growth continues slowly beyond it. Option 3 describes a hypothetical unbounded pool; the maximum is a ceiling, not a growth rate, and the pool never bursts thousands of threads in milliseconds. Option 4 is wrong on both counts: hill climbing is a slow feedback loop that moves the count by small steps based on measured throughput, and the .NET 6+ blocking-aware adjustment only triggers when a pool thread blocks on an incomplete `Task` (`.Wait()`, `.Result`, `GetAwaiter().GetResult()`); a `lock`, `Thread.Sleep` or a synchronous socket call is invisible to it, so the slow path applies.

options.text: Each inner `Task.Run` goes to the *local* queue of the pool thread running the outer delegate; that thread and any idle worker that steals from it share the work.
All four inner tasks go to the single global FIFO queue, exactly as if queued from the main thread, because `TaskScheduler.Default` applies `PreferFairness` to nested tasks.
The inner tasks are executed inline on the current thread because they were created from within a running task, so `Crunch(0..3)` run sequentially on that one worker.
Each inner task gets its own dedicated OS thread because a `Task.Run` issued from inside another task is treated as `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`.

en.explanation: `Task.Run` uses `TaskScheduler.Default`, which queues to the thread pool with `preferLocal` semantics: when the caller is a pool thread the item goes to that thread's local work-stealing queue. The owner pops its local queue LIFO (most recent item first, for cache locality), while idle workers steal from the opposite end (FIFO), so with several free cores the four `Crunch` calls typically run in parallel, some on the originating thread and some on stealers. (The `var n = i;` copy matters: a `for` variable is shared across iterations, so capturing `i` directly would make every call `Crunch(4)`.) Option 2 is what happens for the *outer* `Task.Run`, queued from the main (non-pool) thread; `PreferFairness` does route to the global queue, but it is an explicit `Task.Factory.StartNew` option that `Task.Run` never sets. Option 3 confuses this with task inlining, which the scheduler does only when a thread *blocks waiting* on a not-yet-started task (`Task.Wait`), never at creation time. Option 4 is wrong: `LongRunning` must be requested explicitly through `Task.Factory.StartNew`, and it bypasses the pool entirely by creating a dedicated thread; `Task.Run` has no such overload and nesting changes nothing.

en.prompt: A teammate opens a pull request that wraps every EF Core query in an ASP.NET Core API in `Task.Run(...)`, with the description 'makes the endpoints more parallel and frees the request thread'. Explain to them what actually happens on the thread pool, what the correct approach is, and in which situations `Task.Run` (or a dedicated thread) *is* the right tool.
en.explanation: A strong answer explains that a request handler already executes on a thread pool worker, so `Task.Run` merely relocates the work to another worker from the same pool: no extra capacity, one extra queue hop and context switch, and new hazards because `DbContext` and `HttpContext` are not thread-safe and are scoped to the request. Only a genuinely asynchronous API (`ToListAsync`, `SaveChangesAsync`) frees the thread, because the wait is handed to the OS and the continuation is queued when the I/O completes. The answer should place `Task.Run` where a dedicated caller thread must stay responsive (desktop UI, Blazor Hybrid) or for bounded CPU-heavy work whose competition with other requests is accepted, and route work that should outlive the request through a `Channel<T>` plus `BackgroundService`, or a long-lived loop through `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`/`new Thread`.
rubric: States that ASP.NET Core request handlers already run on thread pool threads, so `Task.Run` only moves the work to another worker of the same pool and adds no capacity (extra queue hop/context switch).
Explains that only a truly asynchronous API (`await db.Users.ToListAsync(ct)` etc.) releases the thread during I/O, because the wait is handled by the OS and the continuation is queued on completion.

Identifies the thread-safety hazard: `DbContext` and `HttpContext` are request-scoped and not thread-safe, so touching them from a `Task.Run` thread (especially one that outlives the response) is a bug.
Names legitimate uses of `Task.Run`: keeping a dedicated UI/render thread responsive (WPF, MAUI, Blazor Hybrid), or bounded CPU-heavy work where competing with other requests is accepted.

Proposes the right tool for work that must outlive the request or run continuously: `Channel<T>` + `BackgroundService`, or `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`/`new Thread` for a long-lived loop, rather than fire-and-forget `Task.Run`.

en.title: Cancellation: tokens, linking, timeouts

options.text: `Faulted Canceled`: only the async state machine turns an `OperationCanceledException` into a cancelled task; `Task.Run` does so only when the exception's token equals the token passed to `Task.Run` and that token is cancelled.
`Canceled Canceled`: throwing `OperationCanceledException` always transitions the task to `Canceled`; that is what the exception type is for.
`Faulted Faulted`: neither exception carries a cancelled token, so the runtime has no evidence of a real cancellation and both tasks fault.
`Canceled Faulted`: `Task.Run` recognises `OperationCanceledException`, but an `async` method needs `Task.FromCanceled` to end up cancelled; a thrown exception always faults it.

en.explanation: `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder.SetException` special-cases *any* `OperationCanceledException` and completes the async method's task with `TrySetCanceled(oce.CancellationToken, oce)`, so `b` is `Canceled` even though its token is `CancellationToken.None`. A plain `Action` delegate run by `Task.Run`/`Task.Factory.StartNew` goes through `Task.HandleException`, which marks the task cancelled only when the exception's `CancellationToken` equals the token that was passed to `Task.Run` *and* that token has cancellation requested; here no token was passed, so `a` is `Faulted`. Option 2 is the async-only rule generalised to all tasks. Option 3 is the delegate-only rule generalised to async methods. Option 4 has both halves backwards; `Task.FromCanceled` is for hand-built tasks, not needed inside an `async` method. Note that `await a` and `await b` both throw `OperationCanceledException`, so the difference is visible only through `Status`, `ContinueWith` options and `Task.WhenAll`, where a faulted sibling takes precedence over a cancelled one. Be aware that `Task.Run(() => { throw ...; })` with a block lambda that never reaches its end binds to the `Func<Task>` overload, whose unwrap promise treats a synchronous OCE as cancellation, so it behaves like the async case; that is why the sample uses method groups.

options.text: `when (ex.CancellationToken == timeoutCts.Token)`: the exception carries the token that caused it, and only the timeout source owns that token.
`when (!callerToken.IsCancellationRequested)`: if the caller did not ask to stop, the only remaining reason for a cancellation coming out of this block is the timeout.
`when (ex is TaskCanceledException)`: timeouts inside `HttpClient` and `Task.Delay` surface as `TaskCanceledException`, while explicit cancellation throws the base `OperationCanceledException`.
`when (ex.CancellationToken == linked.Token)`: the callee received `linked.Token`, so an exception carrying it proves the linked source fired rather than the caller's.

en.explanation: The callee only ever sees `linked.Token`, so the `OperationCanceledException` it throws carries the *linked* token (or, for some libraries, a token of their own). Which upstream source fired is not recorded in the exception; you have to ask the sources. Option 2 asks the right one: if `callerToken` is cancelled, this is a genuine cancellation and must propagate as `Canceled`; if it is not, the cancellation could only have come from the timer. (Checking `timeoutCts.IsCancellationRequested` as well guards against an OCE that arrived for an unrelated token.) Option 1 never matches, because nobody throws with `timeoutCts.Token`; it is the linked token that is handed down. Option 4 is true whichever source fired, since the linked source cancels for both, so it turns every caller cancellation into a `TimeoutException`. Option 3 confuses exception *type* with *reason*: `Task.Delay`, `HttpClient` and `WaitAsync` throw `TaskCanceledException` for ordinary cancellation too, and since .NET 5 an `HttpClient` timeout is a `TaskCanceledException` with a `TimeoutException` inner exception, so the derived type is not a timeout marker.

en.prompt: Which statement about `CancellationTokenSource.Cancel()` and registered callbacks is true?

options.text: By default `Cancel()` runs the registered callbacks synchronously on the calling thread; a callback that throws does not stop the others, and after the loop `Cancel()` throws an `AggregateException`.

Since .NET 8 `Cancel()` queues the callbacks to the thread pool and returns immediately; a callback that throws is reported through `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`, never to the code that called `Cancel()`.
`Cancel()` runs the callbacks synchronously but stops at the first one that throws and rethrows that exception unchanged, because `throwOnFirstException` defaults to `true`.
A callback registered after the token was cancelled is stored and invoked on the next `Cancel()`; since .NET 6 `TryReset()` lets an already-cancelled source be rearmed and cancelled again.

en.explanation: `Cancel()` (which is `Cancel(throwOnFirstException: false)`) flips the state, then invokes the registrations inline on the thread that called it, most recently registered first; the only exception is a registration made with `Register(..., useSynchronizationContext: true)`, which is marshalled through the captured `SynchronizationContext`. Exceptions thrown by callbacks are collected and thrown together as an `AggregateException` after the loop. Because heavy or blocking callbacks therefore make `Cancel()` slow for the caller, .NET 8 added `CancelAsync()`, which returns a task that completes once the callbacks have run. Option 2 describes a design .NET does not use in any version: callbacks are not queued to the pool, and exceptions reach the caller of `Cancel()`, not `UnobservedTaskException`. Option 3 has the default backwards: `throwOnFirstException` defaults to `false`; passing `true` gives the stop-at-first behaviour. Option 4 is wrong twice: registering on an already-cancelled token runs the callback immediately and synchronously inside `Register`, and cancellation is one-way. `TryReset()` (.NET 6) can rearm a source only if it has *not* been cancelled yet, returning `false` otherwise, which is what makes pooling sources possible.

options.text: Replace the return with `Task.Run(() => Checksum(data), ct).WaitAsync(ct)` so the awaiting caller is released as soon as the token fires.
Pass `ct` into `Checksum` and call `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` inside the loop (every N iterations if `Mix` is very cheap); a running delegate is stopped only by code that observes the token.
Call `cts.Cancel(true)` instead of `cts.Cancel()`; the `true` argument tells the runtime to interrupt the thread that is running the delegate.
Use `Task.Factory.StartNew(() => Checksum(data), ct, TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning, TaskScheduler.Default)` so the work gets a dedicated thread that the token can abort.

en.explanation: The token passed to `Task.Run` is consulted once, before the delegate starts: if cancellation is already requested the task completes as `Canceled` without running. Once the loop is executing, nothing outside it can stop it, so the loop itself must poll the token; `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` throws an `OperationCanceledException` carrying `ct`, which matches the token given to `Task.Run`, so the task ends `Canceled` rather than `Faulted`. Option 1 only cancels the *wait*: the caller gets an `OperationCanceledException` while the loop keeps burning a thread-pool thread to the end, which is the sync-over-async cousin of leaking work. Option 3 misreads the parameter: it is `throwOnFirstException`, controlling how callback exceptions are reported, and there is no thread interruption in cancellation at all. Option 4 changes only where the delegate runs; `Thread.Abort` is unsupported on .NET Core and later (it throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`), and a `LongRunning` thread is no more abortable than a pool thread.

en.prompt: An ASP.NET Core endpoint calls a downstream HTTP API, then writes the result to the database inside a transaction, then publishes an event. Design the cancellation story end to end: which tokens exist, how they are combined, what each layer does with `OperationCanceledException`, and where cancellation must stop being honoured. Name the .NET APIs you would use.
rubric: Identifies the sources: `HttpContext.RequestAborted` (bound to the handler's `CancellationToken` parameter, fires on client disconnect), a per-call timeout (`CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan)` / `CancelAfter`), and host shutdown (`IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`), combined with `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource` that is disposed (`using`) so registrations on long-lived tokens do not leak.

Propagates the token through every async call (HttpClient, EF Core/ADO.NET, message publisher) rather than passing `default`/`CancellationToken.None`, and treats CPU-bound loops as needing explicit `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` checkpoints because cancellation is cooperative.

Distinguishes caller cancellation from timeout at the boundary: an OCE when `RequestAborted` is cancelled is not an error (let it propagate / map to a 499-style response, log at low level), while a timeout is a failure surfaced as `TimeoutException` or a 504, using `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (...)` filters on the source tokens (`RequestAborted.IsCancellationRequested`, the timeout source's `IsCancellationRequested`) rather than on the exception's type.

Defines a point of no return: once the transaction is committed (or the external side effect such as a payment is made) the remaining steps run with `CancellationToken.None` or a separate shutdown-only token so the system is not left half-done; optionally mentions outbox/idempotency for the event publish.

Explains how status flows: an `async` method that throws OCE yields a `Canceled` task, catching `OperationCanceledException` (the base type) rather than only `TaskCanceledException`, and throwing `new OperationCanceledException(ct)` so the token identifies the origin.
en.explanation: Model answer outline: the handler receives `RequestAborted` as its `CancellationToken` parameter; the service creates `using var timeoutCts = new CancellationTokenSource(budget)` and `using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(requestAborted, timeoutCts.Token, lifetime.ApplicationStopping)`, passing `cts.Token` to `HttpClient`, EF Core (`BeginTransactionAsync(ct)`, `SaveChangesAsync(ct)`) and the publisher. At the boundary it uses `catch (OperationCanceledException) when (requestAborted.IsCancellationRequested)` to let client disconnects propagate as a cancelled task (typically logged at debug and mapped to a 499-style response by middleware), `catch (OperationCanceledException oce) when (timeoutCts.IsCancellationRequested)` to convert timeouts into `TimeoutException`/504, and treats the remaining case, host shutdown via `ApplicationStopping`, as a failure too (503 or a rethrow that the host handles), never as a timeout. After the transaction commits, publishing the event uses `CancellationToken.None` (or an outbox row written inside the same transaction) so a disconnect cannot leave a committed write without its event. Throughout, OCE is thrown with the token that fired and the base `OperationCanceledException` type is caught, never only `TaskCanceledException`.

en.task:
Implement a static class `Coop` with two operations and one diagnostic counter:

```csharp
public static Task<T> WithTimeoutAsync<T>(Func<CancellationToken, Task<T>> operation, TimeSpan timeout, CancellationToken cancellationToken = default);
public static Task<T> WithCancellationAsync<T>(this Task<T> task, CancellationToken cancellationToken);
public static int LiveRegistrations { get; }   // registrations Coop currently holds on caller-supplied tokens
```

**`WithTimeoutAsync`** runs `operation` with a token that is cancelled when `cancellationToken` is cancelled **or** `timeout` elapses, whichever comes first, and maps the outcome:
- `operation` completes -> its result is returned; any non-cancellation exception propagates unchanged.
- `cancellationToken` was cancelled (whether or not the timer also fired) -> the returned task is **`Canceled`** and awaiting it throws an `OperationCanceledException` whose `CancellationToken == cancellationToken` (the caller's token, not the linked one).
- Only the timer fired -> the returned task is **`Faulted`** with a `TimeoutException` whose `InnerException` is the original `OperationCanceledException`.
- `timeout == Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan` -> no timer and no linked source are created; `operation` receives `cancellationToken` itself. Any other negative `timeout` -> `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- The operation is **never abandoned**: do not race it against a delay and return while it is still running. Cancellation reaches it only through the token.
- No resource leak: the linked source (and its timer and its registration on `cancellationToken`) is disposed on every path.

**`WithCancellationAsync`** makes *waiting* on an existing task cancellable; the task itself is not affected and keeps running.
- `task` already completed, or `cancellationToken.CanBeCanceled == false` -> return `task` itself.
- `cancellationToken` already cancelled -> return a task that is `Canceled` for that token without touching `task`.
- Otherwise: if `task` finishes first, propagate its result/fault/cancellation; if the token fires first, the returned task is `Canceled` with `OperationCanceledException.CancellationToken == cancellationToken`.
- The registration on `cancellationToken` must be removed once `task` wins: after 10,000 calls against a long-lived token that never fires, `Coop.LiveRegistrations` must be `0` and `Cancel()` on that token must run no leftover `Coop` callbacks.
- If the abandoned `task` later faults, its exception must be observed so `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` is not raised.

**`LiveRegistrations`** is incremented when either operation registers on a caller-supplied token (directly or through a linked source) and decremented when that registration is disposed; it must be `0` whenever no returned task is pending. It exists so the leak requirement is observable from `Main`.

**Constraints:** .NET 8 or later, no third-party packages, no `Thread.Abort`, no `Task.Wait()`/`.Result` anywhere (including `Main`). Do not use `Task.WaitAsync` inside `WithCancellationAsync` (you are implementing that idea). Write a `Main` that exercises every bullet above and prints `PASS`/`FAIL` per case.

**Examples**
- `await Coop.WithTimeoutAsync(ct => Task.FromResult(1), TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))` -> `1`
- `Coop.WithTimeoutAsync(async ct => { await Task.Delay(-1, ct); return 0; }, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(50))` -> task `Faulted`, exception `TimeoutException { InnerException: OperationCanceledException }`
- With a caller `CancellationTokenSource` cancelled after 50 ms and a 5 s timeout -> task `Canceled`, `oce.CancellationToken == caller.Token`
- `new TaskCompletionSource<int>().Task.WithCancellationAsync(new CancellationTokenSource(50).Token)` -> task `Canceled` after ~50 ms
- After the 10,000-race loop: `Coop.LiveRegistrations == 0`
rubric: `WithTimeoutAsync` creates a linked source only for a finite timeout, uses `CancelAfter` (or the `TimeSpan` constructor), and disposes it on every path (`using`), so no registration accumulates on the caller's token.

Outcome mapping is correct: caller cancellation is rethrown as an `OperationCanceledException` carrying the caller's token (task `Canceled`, checked via `callerToken.IsCancellationRequested` in an exception filter), timeout becomes a `Faulted` task with `TimeoutException` wrapping the OCE, other exceptions propagate unchanged, and the operation is awaited to completion rather than raced against `Task.Delay`.

`WithCancellationAsync` handles the fast paths (completed task, non-cancellable token, already-cancelled token via `Task.FromCanceled<T>`), completes with the caller's token when it fires, and never mutates or cancels the underlying task.

The registration returned by `Register`/`UnsafeRegister` is disposed when the task wins (a `using` or `finally`), `LiveRegistrations` is incremented after registering and decremented on the same path that disposes, and the abandoned task's fault is observed with a continuation.

`Main` demonstrates each contract bullet with observable checks (`Status`, exception type and `CancellationToken` identity, `Coop.LiveRegistrations == 0` after many races, no `UnobservedTaskException` from an abandoned task), uses no `.Wait()`/`.Result`, and the code compiles without warnings.

concepts.title: Concurrency primitives: lock, Lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, ReaderWriterLockSlim, Channel<T>

en.title: Concurrency primitives: lock, Lock, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, ReaderWriterLockSlim, Channel<T>

options.text: It compiles; the lock is released at the `await` and re-acquired when the continuation resumes, so the cache stays consistent.
It compiles but deadlocks at runtime, because the continuation tries to re-enter a Monitor that its own thread already holds.
It does not compile: the C# compiler rejects `await` inside the body of a `lock` statement (CS1996).
It compiles and runs, but throws `SynchronizationLockException` at the closing brace whenever the continuation resumes on a different thread.

en.explanation: `lock` expands to `Monitor.Enter`/`Monitor.Exit` and Monitor ownership is thread-affine; a continuation after `await` may run on any thread pool thread, so the compiler refuses to emit code that could `Exit` from the wrong thread and reports CS1996 instead. The 'released at the await and re-acquired' option describes something the language never does: `lock` has no release-and-reacquire semantics around `await`. The 'deadlocks re-entering its own Monitor' option is wrong twice over: Monitor is reentrant (the same thread can re-enter freely), and the code never runs because it does not compile. The `SynchronizationLockException` option is the behaviour you would get if you wrote `Monitor.Enter`/`Exit` by hand around an `await`, but the `lock` statement never gets that far because it is a compile-time error. The idiomatic fix is a `SemaphoreSlim(1,1)` with `WaitAsync`, or moving the `await` outside the critical section.

en.prompt: Which statement about the `System.Threading.Lock` type introduced with C# 13 / .NET 9 is correct?

options.text: `Lock` is a thin wrapper over `Monitor`: `lock (myLock)` still emits `Monitor.Enter`/`Exit` on the object-header sync block, and the only gain is that analyzers can flag `lock (this)` and `lock (typeof(T))`.

When the operand is statically typed as `Lock`, `lock (x)` compiles to `using (x.EnterScope())`; locking the same instance through an `object` reference uses `Monitor` and does not exclude `EnterScope` callers.

`Lock` is awaitable: because `EnterScope()` returns a disposable scope instead of relying on thread ownership, `await` inside `lock (myLock) { ... }` is legal and the scope is released while the continuation is pending.
Unlike `Monitor`, `Lock` is non-reentrant: like `ReaderWriterLockSlim` with `NoRecursion`, a second `Enter` from the owning thread throws `LockRecursionException` instead of counting the recursion.

en.explanation: The compiler special-cases `Lock`: it emits `EnterScope()` returning a `ref struct` `Scope` whose `Dispose` exits the lock, bypassing the object-header sync block entirely. If the same `Lock` is boxed or passed as `object` and locked, that code uses `Monitor` on the object, a completely separate mechanism, so the two paths do not exclude each other; the compiler warns with CS9216 when it can see the conversion. The 'thin wrapper over Monitor' option is wrong because the code generation is different and the sync-block-free implementation is the whole point. The 'awaitable' option is wrong: `Lock` remains a blocking, thread-affine primitive and `await` inside its body is still rejected with CS1996; an awaitable mutex is still `SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync`. The 'non-reentrant' option is wrong because `Lock` supports recursion just like `Monitor`; the non-reentrant primitives in the toolbox are `SemaphoreSlim` and `ReaderWriterLockSlim` (by default).

en.prompt: A service uses `private readonly SemaphoreSlim _gate = new(1, 1);` around an `await`-ing critical section as an async mutex. Which statement is true?

options.text: Like `Monitor`, `SemaphoreSlim` records the owning thread, so nested `Wait` calls from that thread pass through and `Release()` throws if it runs on a thread other than the acquirer.
`WaitAsync()` parks a thread pool thread until a slot is free, so under contention it exhausts the pool exactly as `Wait()` would; its only advantage is cancellation support.
Calling `Release()` more times than `Wait()` is harmless: the count is clamped at `maxCount`, which is why releasing from a `finally` is safe even when `WaitAsync` was cancelled before acquiring.
No thread affinity: `Release()` may run on whatever thread the continuation resumed on; but not reentrant, so re-entering on the same logical flow deadlocks.

en.explanation: A semaphore counts slots, it does not know who owns them: that is what makes it usable across `await` (the continuation may be on a different thread) and what makes it non-reentrant (a second `WaitAsync` on the same flow sees zero slots and waits forever). The 'records the owning thread' option describes Monitor/`Lock` semantics, not `SemaphoreSlim`, which is precisely why `SemaphoreSlim` works where `lock` cannot. The 'parks a thread pool thread' option is wrong: `WaitAsync` returns an incomplete `Task` and the caller yields; no thread is blocked, which is the entire reason to prefer it in async code. The 'clamped at maxCount' option is wrong because releasing past `maxCount` throws `SemaphoreFullException`; a cancelled `WaitAsync` never acquired a slot, so releasing in a `finally` for it is a bug, and a missing `Release` (no `try`/`finally` around code that did acquire) leaks the slot permanently.

en.prompt: A producer writes into `Channel.CreateBounded<Job>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait })` and the single consumer stalls for a minute. What happens to producers once 100 items are queued?

options.text: `WriteAsync` returns an incomplete `ValueTask` and the producer awaits until the consumer frees a slot (backpressure); `TryWrite` returns `false` without blocking.
`WriteAsync` throws `ChannelClosedException`, because a bounded channel treats a full buffer as a terminal state and the writer has to be recreated.
The channel switches to unbounded mode and keeps buffering in a linked list, so the producer never observes the slow consumer.
The oldest queued item is discarded to make room, because dropping the oldest item is the default behaviour of a bounded channel.

en.explanation: `BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait` (the default) is exactly how a bounded channel propagates backpressure: writers asynchronously wait for capacity, and `TryWrite` reports `false` so a caller can shed load itself. `ChannelClosedException` is raised only after `Writer.Complete()` or `TryComplete()` has been called, never because the buffer is full, so the 'terminal state' option is wrong. A bounded channel never grows past its capacity; unbounded growth is the failure mode of `CreateUnbounded<T>()`, which is why bounded channels are preferred in servers, so the 'switches to unbounded mode' option is wrong. Dropping is available but must be opted into with `DropOldest`, `DropNewest` or `DropWrite`; it is not the default, so the 'oldest item is discarded' option is wrong.

en.prompt: You maintain an in-process configuration cache: thousands of reads per second from request threads, and a refresh every few minutes that fetches new values over HTTP. Compare implementing it with `lock`/`Lock`, `ReaderWriterLockSlim`, and an immutable snapshot swapped with `Interlocked`/`Volatile`. Which would you choose and why, and how do you keep the asynchronous refresh from running concurrently with itself?
en.explanation: Model answer: the read path should be lock-free. Keep the whole configuration in one immutable object and read it through a single field (`Volatile.Read` or a plain reference read; reference assignment is atomic, so readers never see torn state). The refresher builds a new snapshot off-line and publishes it with `Interlocked.Exchange` or `Volatile.Write`. `ReaderWriterLockSlim` would let readers run concurrently but is thread-affine, not awaitable and adds bookkeeping that only pays off for long read-mostly critical sections; here the critical section is a single reference read, so `lock`/`Lock` would already be as fast and the snapshot swap is faster still. The refresh awaits an HTTP call, so it cannot sit inside `lock`, `Lock` (CS1996) or `ReaderWriterLockSlim` (thread-affine); guard it with `SemaphoreSlim(1,1).WaitAsync` in `try`/`finally` so a second trigger waits or skips instead of fetching twice, remembering that the semaphore is not reentrant and that an exception must still release it. If the invariant ever spans several independently updated fields, `Interlocked` on one word no longer suffices: either bundle them in the immutable snapshot or fall back to a lock.
rubric: States that `ReaderWriterLockSlim` allows concurrent readers but is thread-affine, not awaitable and carries bookkeeping overhead, so it only pays off for long read-mostly critical sections; for a short 'read a reference' section a plain `lock` or `Lock` is usually as fast or faster.

Proposes the immutable-snapshot pattern: readers read a single reference (`Volatile.Read` or a plain read of a reference), the refresher builds a new object and publishes it with `Interlocked.Exchange`/`Volatile.Write`, giving lock-free reads and no torn state because a reference assignment is atomic.

Explains that the refresh cannot hold `lock`/`Lock`/`ReaderWriterLockSlim` across the HTTP `await` (compile error or thread-affinity violation) and guards it with `SemaphoreSlim(1,1).WaitAsync` in a `try`/`finally`, or an equivalent non-reentrant async gate, so overlapping refreshes coalesce rather than run twice.
Notes that `Interlocked` only covers a single word: if the cache invariant spans several fields, either bundle them in one immutable object that is swapped atomically or fall back to a lock.

Mentions at least one concrete pitfall: `ReaderWriterLockSlim` defaults to `NoRecursion` and throws `LockRecursionException` on re-entry, `SemaphoreSlim` is not reentrant, or an exception inside the refresh must still release the gate.

concepts.title: Parallel vs async: CPU-bound vs IO-bound

en.title: Parallel vs async: CPU-bound vs IO-bound

options.text: The downloads run in parallel and `Parallel.ForEach` waits for all of them; the log line is accurate but the calling thread is blocked for the whole duration.
`ForEach` returns once every lambda hits its first `await`; the log line is written early and download exceptions are unobserved `async void` faults that can crash the process.
The code does not compile because `Parallel.ForEach` has no overload that accepts an async lambda.
`Parallel.ForEach` recognises the returned `Task` objects and awaits them internally, so behaviour is equivalent to `Task.WhenAll` without a degree-of-parallelism limit.

en.explanation: The `(source, body)` overloads of `Parallel.ForEach` take `Action<T>`, so the async lambda is compiled as `async void`. The method returns when every lambda has *started* and hit its first incomplete `await`; the remaining work continues on thread-pool threads with nobody observing it. Exceptions from an `async void` method are posted to the `SynchronizationContext` or, in ASP.NET Core / console apps, thrown on the pool and terminate the process. The first option is wrong because `ForEach` does not wait; it has no `Task` to wait on. The third option is wrong because an async lambda converts to `Action<T>` (as `async void`) without error, which is exactly the trap. The fourth option is wrong because nothing is returned to `ForEach`: the lambda's return type is `void`, so there are no tasks to await. The correct replacement is `Parallel.ForEachAsync` (.NET 6+) with an explicit `MaxDegreeOfParallelism`.

en.prompt: You call `Parallel.ForEachAsync(items, async (item, ct) => await client.SendAsync(item, ct))` on a 32-core server without passing `ParallelOptions`. Which statement about the degree of parallelism is true?

options.text: There is no limit: like `Parallel.ForEach` with default options, `ForEachAsync` lets the scheduler decide, so all items are started immediately.
Items are processed one at a time because an async body cannot be safely overlapped without an explicit `MaxDegreeOfParallelism`.
At most `Environment.ProcessorCount` (32) operations are in flight at once; `ForEachAsync` maps the default `-1` to the processor count, and awaiting operations hold no pool thread.
The limit equals `ThreadPool.GetMinThreads()`, because each in-flight operation permanently occupies one pool thread until it completes.

en.explanation: `ParallelOptions.MaxDegreeOfParallelism` defaults to `-1`; `Parallel.ForEachAsync` maps that to `Environment.ProcessorCount`, so 32 bodies are started and a new one is dequeued each time one completes. Because the bodies await, the threads are returned to the pool during the IO wait; the limit caps *operations*, not threads. The first option is wrong: it describes the synchronous `Parallel.ForEach`, where `-1` means unlimited; `ForEachAsync` deliberately defaults to the core count so that unthrottled fan-out is opt-in. The second option is wrong: the whole point of `ForEachAsync` is overlapping async bodies; sequential processing would be a plain `foreach` with `await`. The fourth option is wrong: an awaiting operation holds no thread, so pool size is unrelated to the concurrency limit. Note that for IO-bound work `ProcessorCount` is an arbitrary default; you should set the limit from the downstream dependency's capacity.

en.prompt: A repository exposes `IAsyncEnumerable<Order> GetOrdersAsync(CancellationToken ct)` implemented with `await reader.ReadAsync(ct)` and `yield return`. Which statement about consuming it with `await foreach` is correct?

options.text: The compiler-generated iterator runs all `ReadAsync` calls concurrently and buffers the results, so `await foreach` is a faster drop-in for `ToListAsync()`.
`await foreach` executes the loop body for several items at once, up to `Environment.ProcessorCount`, which is why it is preferred over `Task<List<T>>` for large result sets.
Calling `.ToListAsync()` on the enumerable keeps the streaming behaviour because the list is populated incrementally as the caller enumerates it.
Items are pulled one at a time: each `MoveNextAsync()` is awaited before the body runs, so the first order arrives before the query finishes and memory stays bounded, but nothing runs in parallel.

en.explanation: `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is a pull-based, lazy, sequential protocol: the consumer awaits `MoveNextAsync()`, gets one item, runs the body, and only then asks for the next. Its benefits are early first item and bounded memory, not parallelism. The first option is wrong because the iterator state machine executes strictly one step at a time; there is no concurrent prefetch. The second option is wrong because `await foreach` never runs the body concurrently; that is what `Parallel.ForEachAsync` (which accepts an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`) or a `Channel<T>` with multiple readers is for. The third option is wrong because `ToListAsync()` materialises the whole sequence before returning, so the caller waits for the last row and holds everything in memory, discarding exactly the advantage of streaming.

en.prompt: A batch job runs `await Task.WhenAll(ids.Select(id => enrichApi.FetchAsync(id)))` over 50,000 ids. The external API allows 20 concurrent requests per client and starts returning HTTP 429 within seconds. Which fix is correct?

options.text: Replace it with `Parallel.ForEachAsync(ids, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 20 }, ...)` or a `SemaphoreSlim(20)` gate, so at most 20 requests are in flight regardless of core count.
Replace it with `Parallel.ForEach(ids, id => enrichApi.FetchAsync(id).GetAwaiter().GetResult())`, which limits concurrency to the number of cores and keeps the code synchronous.
Keep `Task.WhenAll` and call `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads(20, 20)` so the runtime schedules only 20 requests at a time.
Use `ids.AsParallel().WithDegreeOfParallelism(20).Select(id => enrichApi.FetchAsync(id))` and await the resulting tasks; PLINQ enforces the limit on the async calls.

en.explanation: `Task.WhenAll` over a `Select` starts every request immediately; nothing throttles it. The problem is *concurrency* against an IO dependency, so the fix is a concurrency limit set from the dependency's capacity: `Parallel.ForEachAsync` with `MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 20` or a `SemaphoreSlim` gate. The second option is wrong on two counts: it turns async IO into sync-over-async that blocks one thread-pool thread per in-flight request (the .NET 6+ pool detects Task-blocking and injects threads faster, but that only adds more blocked threads, not a limit), and the default degree for `Parallel.ForEach` is unlimited, not the core count, so it does not even guarantee 20. The third option is wrong because `SetMinThreads` controls how many threads the pool creates without delay; it has no effect on how many already-started tasks are in flight, and awaiting requests do not hold threads anyway. The fourth option is wrong because PLINQ limits how many *`Select` invocations* run concurrently, and each invocation returns instantly with a hot `Task`; the HTTP calls themselves are still all started at once.

en.prompt: You must process 2 million rows from PostgreSQL: for each row call an external enrichment API (rate-limited to 50 concurrent requests), compute a SHA-256 over the merged payload, and write the result to blob storage. Memory is capped at 512 MB and the job must be cancellable. Describe how you would structure this in .NET 10, which parts are CPU-bound versus IO-bound, how you would choose and set degree of parallelism, and what happens when one API call throws.
en.explanation: A strong answer separates the IO-bound stages (DB read, API call, blob write) from the CPU-bound hash, streams the rows instead of loading them, bounds concurrency by the API's capacity rather than by cores, propagates one `CancellationToken` through every stage, and explains the failure semantics of the chosen fan-out primitive. Reading rows through `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (`ReadAsync` + `yield return`) keeps memory bounded; `Parallel.ForEachAsync` over that stream with `MaxDegreeOfParallelism = 50` throttles the API; the hash is cheap enough to run inline on the continuation, or, if it were heavy, would be a separate CPU-bound stage bounded by `ProcessorCount`; on the first exception `ForEachAsync` stops dequeuing, cancels the body token for in-flight items, and faults, so the answer should decide whether to catch per item (log and continue) or let the job fail.
rubric: Reads rows as a stream (`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` / `DbDataReader.ReadAsync` with `yield return`, or a bounded `Channel<T>`) rather than materialising 2 million rows into a list, and ties that to the 512 MB limit.

Correctly classifies the DB read, API call and blob write as IO-bound (async, no thread held while waiting) and the SHA-256 as CPU-bound, and explains that CPU-bound work does not benefit from `await`.

Uses `Parallel.ForEachAsync` (or `SemaphoreSlim`/`Channel<T>` workers) with the degree of parallelism set to the API's limit (50), stating explicitly that for IO the limit comes from downstream capacity, not `Environment.ProcessorCount`.

Ensures the same token reaches the row enumerator (as a plain parameter, via `[EnumeratorCancellation]`/`WithCancellation`, or via `ParallelOptions.CancellationToken`, which `ForEachAsync` forwards to `GetAsyncEnumerator`), every API/blob call, and `ParallelOptions`.

Describes failure semantics: `Parallel.ForEachAsync` stops dequeuing and cancels the body token when an iteration throws, then the returned task faults; states whether errors are caught per item (retry/skip and log) or allowed to fail the job, and does not rely on `Parallel.ForEach` with an async lambda or sync-over-async.

concepts.title: Async pitfalls: async void, sync-over-async, WhenAll and fire-and-forget

en.title: Async pitfalls: async void, sync-over-async, WhenAll and fire-and-forget

options.text: `ForEach` awaits each `SendAsync` in turn before returning, so the exception propagates out of `ForEach`, through the endpoint and the exception-handling middleware, and the client receives a 500 instead of 202.

The compiler-generated state machine catches the exception, wraps it in an `AggregateException` and rethrows it at the `ForEach` call site, where the exception-handling middleware turns it into a 500 response.

The lambda is compiled as `async void` because `ForEach` takes `Action<T>`; the endpoint returns 202, and the exception is rethrown on a thread-pool thread as an unhandled exception that terminates the process.

The lambda's task is created but never awaited, so the exception is held inside it and raised later through `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` when the task is finalized; the process keeps running.

en.explanation: Option 3 is correct. `List<T>.ForEach(Action<T>)` forces the async lambda into an `async void` delegate: there is no `Task` to fault, and `ForEach` returns as soon as each lambda yields at its first `await`, so the 202 is sent long before any send completes. When the exception occurs, `AsyncVoidMethodBuilder.SetException` posts it to the `SynchronizationContext` captured when the lambda started — and ASP.NET Core MVC/minimal APIs have none — so it is rethrown on a thread-pool thread, where an unhandled exception terminates the process. Option 1 is wrong because nothing awaits the lambdas: all sends start concurrently and `ForEach` returns after each one yields. Option 2 is wrong because `ForEach` returns `void`; there is no task whose fault could be wrapped in `AggregateException` or observed by middleware, and by the time the exception occurs the request has usually already completed. Option 4 is wrong because `UnobservedTaskException` applies only to `Task`-returning fire-and-forget calls such as `_ = SendAsync(...)`; an `async void` method produces no `Task` to be finalized, so the exception has nowhere to hide.

options.text: `ex` is an `AggregateException` whose `InnerExceptions` holds both the `InvalidOperationException` and the `TimeoutException`, because `Task.WhenAll` aggregates every faulted input and `await` rethrows that aggregate unchanged to the caller.

The `catch` block runs after roughly 10 ms with the `TimeoutException`, because `Task.WhenAll` faults as soon as its first input faults and stops waiting for the remaining tasks, which keep running unobserved.

The `catch` block runs only after `t3` completes (about 2 s), and `ex` is the unwrapped `InvalidOperationException` — first in input order; the `TimeoutException` is reachable only via `t2.Exception` or the combined task.

After all three complete, `ex` is the `InvalidOperationException`, and the `TimeoutException` from `t2` is left unobserved and later raised through `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` once `t2` is garbage-collected and finalized.

en.explanation: Option 3 is correct on both counts. `Task.WhenAll` completes only when every input has completed, so the `catch` cannot run before `t3` finishes. Its combined task is `Faulted` with an `AggregateException` holding both exceptions in input order, but `await` (via `TaskAwaiter.GetResult()`) rethrows only the first inner exception, unwrapped; to see the second you must keep a reference to the `WhenAll` task and read `Exception.InnerExceptions`, or inspect `t2.Exception`. Option 1 is the most common misconception: the combined task's `Exception` property is indeed an `AggregateException`, but `await` never surfaces it as such. Option 2 is wrong because `WhenAll` never short-circuits — it neither cancels nor abandons the remaining tasks; fail-fast requires cancelling them yourself or using `Task.WhenEach` (.NET 9). Option 4 is wrong because `WhenAll` reads each faulted input's exceptions while building the aggregate, which marks them as observed; nothing reaches `UnobservedTaskException`.

en.prompt: An ASP.NET Core Web API calls a downstream service with `_client.GetFromJsonAsync<Quote>(url).Result` inside a controller action. In production, under load, p99 latency climbs steadily and requests start timing out; CPU stays low and there is no deadlock. Which explanation and fix are correct?

options.text: The request thread is blocked; wrap the call as `Task.Run(() => _client.GetFromJsonAsync<Quote>(url)).Result` so the wait happens on a background pool thread and the request thread is released while the HTTP call is in flight.

No `SynchronizationContext`, so no deadlock; each blocked request pins a pool thread while its continuation needs another, and the pool injects replacement threads slowly. Fix: make the call chain `async` end to end and `await`.

`.Result` blocks because it goes through `Task.Wait`, whereas `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` registers a continuation and yields the thread; switching every `.Result` to `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` removes the latency growth without changing signatures.

The pool starts at `MinThreads` = processor count and only grows on demand; raising `ThreadPool.SetMinThreads` to a few hundred at startup removes the starvation permanently and is the recommended fix when the code cannot be made `async`.

en.explanation: Option 2 is correct. Without a `SynchronizationContext` (true for MVC and minimal APIs; Blazor Server is the exception) the continuation can run on any pool thread, so no deadlock occurs, but every blocked request consumes a thread for the whole downstream round-trip. Once demand exceeds `MinThreads`, the pool's starvation-avoidance path adds roughly one thread per 500 ms — hill-climbing is the throughput tuner and does not rescue a starving pool — which is exactly the slow staircase in p99. The only real fix is to remove the block. Option 1 gains nothing: `Task.Run(...).Result` still blocks the request thread for the entire call and merely adds a thread-pool hop; the extra thread is held only until the delegate's first `await`, so it is not a second long-held thread, but the original one is still stuck. Option 3 is wrong because `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` blocks exactly like `.Result`; the only difference is that it rethrows the first exception unwrapped instead of inside an `AggregateException`. Option 4 is a band-aid, not a fix: a higher minimum lets the pool skip the slow injection phase up to that limit, but each blocked request still burns a thread and starvation returns once load exceeds the new floor. Note that since .NET 6 the pool detects threads blocked in `Task.Wait`/`.Result` and injects faster, which is why the symptom is milder than on .NET Core 3.1 — but still present.

options.text: The unobserved exception escalates when the task's finalizer runs and terminates the process, so the outage appears as a crash a few seconds after the request; wrapping the body of `ReindexAsync` in `try/catch` is enough to prevent it.

The discard keeps the task rooted and marks its exception as observed, so failures are logged by the hosting layer; `_db` stays alive because the container keeps the request scope open until every task started inside it completes.

The task inherits `HttpContext.RequestAborted` and is cancelled when the response completes, so no `ObjectDisposedException` can occur; the only issue is that the client never learns whether reindexing succeeded.

`_ =` only suppresses warning CS4014; the request's DI scope is disposed when the response completes, so the continuation typically fails with `ObjectDisposedException` on `_db`, and that exception surfaces at most through `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`.

en.explanation: Option 4 is correct. The discard is purely a compile-time silencer; the task runs unobserved, the request scope (and with it `_db`) is disposed when the response ends, and the continuation lands on a disposed context. Because nothing awaits the task, the exception stays inside it until the `TaskExceptionHolder` finalizer raises `UnobservedTaskException` — a silent failure unless you subscribe to that event. The robust replacement is to enqueue the work (a `Channel<T>` or an external queue) and process it in a `BackgroundService` that creates its own `IServiceScope` and links cancellation to `IHostApplicationLifetime`. Option 1 describes .NET Framework 4.0 behaviour; since 4.5, and in .NET Core/.NET 5+, unobserved task exceptions are raised on the event and swallowed by default (the opt-in `ThrowUnobservedTaskExceptions` runtime switch restores the crash, but it is off unless you set it); a `try/catch` inside `ReindexAsync` would also not stop `_db` from being disposed underneath it. Option 2 is wrong on every claim: the discard does not root, observe or log anything, and DI scopes are tied to the request, not to outstanding tasks. Option 3 is wrong because cancellation never flows implicitly — nothing links the task to `RequestAborted` unless you pass that token — and even if it did, cancellation would not prevent the scope-disposal race.
